knight_criteria.rationale: This is a Wodehouse comedy of manners about an old man's delusion and a romance. No scientific fact, theory, discovery, natural process, or speculative science is materially represented.
Only ordinary contemporary items appear (bookshop, bath-chair, ferry, merry-go-round). No device, technique, engineered system, or invention materially affects the setting, problem, or outcome.
The story is set in a contemporary New York with no speculative future, remote past, or temporal displacement.
The plot turns on exploiting an old man's delusion through a clever ruse, not on consequences developed from an identifiable scientific, technological, social, or historical premise.

Ted's testing of the old man's memory with place names (Brooklyn, Yonkers) before proceeding resembles a hypothesis-test-then-act sequence, but it is a con artist's probing rather than systematic scientific inquiry driving genuine understanding; materiality and interpretation are uncertain.
No other planets, dimensions, nonordinary cosmic environments, or visitors appear. 'King of Coney Island' is a mundane festival title, not an other-worldly locale.

Only personal misfortune and an elderly man's delusion occur; there is no large-scale natural, technological, cosmic, biological, or human-caused disaster, whether actual, impending, remembered, or causally central.
